request.system:
You revise one blog article for an online shop. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, the current draft, and the problems found in it. Return the whole article again with every problem fixed. Where a sentence cannot be backed by a fact, remove it or say less; never add a citation the fact does not support. Keep what was good.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

Title: How to Use a French Press: A Step-by-Step Guide to a Clean, Full-Bodied Cup
Meta description: Learn how to use a French press step by step: ratio, coarse grind, water temperature, steep time and plunging for a clean, full-bodied cup.
Slug: how-to-use-a-french-press

To use a French press, weigh roughly 1 g of coarsely ground coffee for every 15–16 g of water. Pour water just off the boil over the grounds, stir, and steep for about 4 minutes. Then skim the crust, press the plunger slowly and pour every drop out straight away [G]. Each step below explains why it matters, so you can get a cup with plenty of body but very little sludge.

## Why the French Press Makes Such a Full-Bodied Cup

A French press is an immersion brewer. Instead of water flowing through a bed of coffee, as in pour-over, all the grounds sit in all the water for the whole brew. Extraction happens evenly and gently, which makes the method forgiving and easy to repeat.

After the steep, a metal mesh pushes the grounds to the bottom. Paper filters trap coffee oils and most fine particles. Metal mesh lets a share of both through, and that gives French press coffee its rich, rounded texture. The trade-off is sediment, so most of the technique below is about keeping body while limiting grit.

[Our French Press](P1) is an immersion brewer with a borosilicate glass beaker held in a stainless steel frame [F2, F4, F5]. Its plunger carries a four-layer mesh filter [F7].

{{P1}}

## What You Need: Ratio, Water and Batch Size

A good French press cup comes from a few simple measurements. Work by weight rather than scoops, because bean density and grind size make volume unreliable.

- **Ratio:** start at around 1:15 to 1:16 coffee to water, for example 60–65 g of coffee to 1 litre of water [G].
- **Water temperature:** just off the boil, roughly 93–96 °C, or about 30 seconds after the kettle clicks off [G].
- **Scale and timer:** a scale makes the ratio repeatable, and a timer keeps the steep consistent.
- **Fresh, coarse grounds:** see the next section.

Our French Press holds 1 litre and makes about 4 mugs [F1, F6]. For a full press, the 60–65 g to 1 litre starting point above works well. For a smaller batch, keep the same ratio and scale both numbers down. For example, 30 g of coffee to 500 g of water gives the same strength in half the volume [G]. Fill the beaker to below the rim so there is space for the crust and for stirring.

If your first cup tastes too strong or too weak, change the ratio before anything else. Leave the grind and time alone for now, so you change one variable at a time.

## Get the Grind Right: Coarse and Even

Grind size matters more in a French press than almost anything else.

- **Too fine:** fine particles slip through the mesh and keep extracting in your cup. The result is a muddy, bitter brew, and the plunger is hard to push.
- **Too coarse:** the water cannot extract enough in the steep time, and the cup tastes thin, sour and hollow.
- **Just right:** grounds look like coarse sea salt or rough breadcrumbs, with particles of similar size.

Evenness matters as much as size. Blade grinders smash beans into a mix of dust and chunks, so you get bitterness and sourness in the same cup. A burr grinder crushes beans between two burrs set at a fixed gap, which gives a far more consistent particle size. Grind just before brewing, because ground coffee loses its aromatics quickly.

[Our Hand Grinder](P2) is a manual grinder with 38 mm hardened stainless steel conical burrs [F11, F12]. It has external click adjustment with 30 settings, ranging from espresso to French press [F13, F14]. That means the coarse end of the dial is built for this brew method.

The Hand Grinder holds 25 g of beans, so a full-press dose needs grinding in batches [F15]. Weigh your total dose first, then grind it in loads and tip each one into the beaker. Every batch then comes out at the same setting. More options are in our [grinders collection](L1).

{{P2}}

## Step by Step: Bloom, Steep, Break the Crust, Plunge

Once your coffee is weighed and ground, the brew itself takes only a few minutes.

1. **Preheat.** Swirl some hot water in the beaker and discard it. A cold glass beaker pulls heat from the brew.
2. **Add the grounds.** Put the beaker on your scale, tip in the coffee and tare.
3. **Pour all the water.** Pour steadily so every ground gets wet, up to your target weight. The coffee will foam and form a crust as trapped gas escapes. This is the bloom.
4. **Stir gently.** Give it a few slow stirs with a spoon to break up dry clumps. Then fit the lid with the plunger raised, to hold in heat.
5. **Steep for 4 minutes.** This is the standard starting point for a coarse grind [G].
6. **Break and skim the crust.** Take off the lid and stir the surface crust gently so the grounds sink. Then spoon off the foam and floating bits that remain. This step removes much of what would otherwise end up as grit and bitterness in your cup.
7. **Optional: wait a few minutes more.** Leaving the brew for a few extra minutes lets the fine particles settle to the bottom. Extraction slows a lot once the grounds have sunk, so the cup gets cleaner rather than more bitter.
8. **Press slowly.** Lower the plunger with light, steady pressure, and stop just above the bed of grounds. Pressing hard or all the way down stirs up the settled fines and squeezes bitterness out of the grounds.

On our French Press, the four-layer mesh filter does the separating as you press [F7]. A slow, gentle push gives it the best chance to hold back the grounds.

## Pour Immediately for a Cleaner Cup

The plunger separates the grounds, but they are still in contact with the coffee at the bottom of the beaker. If you leave the brew sitting, it keeps extracting and turns harsh. Pour all the coffee out as soon as you have pressed, into mugs or a carafe.

Leave the last centimetre or so behind. That final pour holds most of the sediment, and stopping short is the easiest way to get a clean cup.

When your first brew is done, adjust one variable at a time:

| What you taste | Likely cause | What to change |
|---|---|---|
| Bitter, drying, harsh | Over-extraction | Grind coarser or shorten the steep |
| Sour, thin, hollow | Under-extraction | Grind finer or lengthen the steep |
| Muddy, gritty | Too many fines | Grind coarser, skim the crust, let it settle, press more gently |
| Too strong or too weak | Ratio | Use less or more coffee for the same water |

## Choosing Beans for French Press

The press's heavy body suits coffees with sweetness and depth, though brighter coffees can work very well too. Browse the full range in our [coffee beans collection](L2).

For a classic, rounded French press cup, [our Colombia Huila](P3) is a washed-process medium roast [F19, F28]. Its tasting notes are red apple, caramel and milk chocolate [F30]. These sweet, chocolatey flavours sit naturally with the press's full texture. It comes in 250 g and 1 kg sizes [F22].

{{P3}}

For a more vivid cup, try [our Ethiopia Guji, natural process](P4). It is a light roast with notes of blueberry, dark chocolate and jasmine [F40, F41]. Immersion brings out its fruit and body together. It is available in 250 g and 1 kg sizes, as whole bean, filter grind or espresso grind [F33, F34]. For French press, choose whole bean and grind coarse at home, because the filter grind is finer than this brew method needs.

{{P4}}

Whatever you choose, buy whole bean where you can and grind fresh for each brew. Pre-ground coffee is rarely coarse enough for a press, and it goes stale faster.

## Cleaning and Care

A clean press is part of a clean cup.

- **Discard the grounds properly.** Scoop or knock them into a compost bin or food waste. Do not rinse them down the sink, where they can build up and clog pipes.
- **Rinse after every brew.** Rinse the beaker and plunger in warm water before coffee oils dry on.
- **Take the plunger apart regularly.** Oils and fines collect between the layers of the mesh. Left there, they turn rancid and give later brews a stale, bitter edge.

All parts of our French Press come apart for cleaning [F8]. Unscrew the plunger assembly every few brews and wash each piece in warm, soapy water. Then rinse thoroughly so no soap taste remains. If the glass breaks, you do not need a whole new brewer, because the French Press beaker is replaceable [F9].

If you enjoy immersion brewing, see the rest of our [immersion brewers collection](L3) for other ways to steep.
